result.summary: Pausanias continues his tour of Sparta and Amyclae, noting statues, temples of Athene the Eye-preserver, Ammon and Cnagian Artemis, and the river Tiasa. He then describes the tripods at Amyclae and, at length, the carved scenes on Bathycles' throne of Amyclaean Apollo.

scenes.title: Sparta's temples and their stories
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists statues and temples near Sparta: Aphrodite, Sleep and Death, Athene the Eye-preserver, Ammon and Cnagian Artemis. He tells the founding tales and doubts the Aphidna story.

scenes.title: Road to Amyclae and its tripods
scenes.summary: On the road to Amyclae lie the river Tiasa and the temple of the Graces. At Amyclae are the statue of Aenetus and the tripods by several sculptors.

scenes.title: The throne of Amyclaean Apollo
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the many mythological scenes carved on Bathycles' throne, outside and underneath.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias stresses he writes as an eyewitness of the throne.

analysis.text: Pausanias pairs sacred sites with local aetiological stories, and he critically tests them, as with the Aphidna tale.
The throne's crowded myth scenes show how Archaic Greek art served as a catalogue of shared legend.

fun_facts.text: The Amyclae throne, known only from Pausanias' description, has prompted much scholarly reconstruction.

language_notes.text: Homer calls Sleep and Death twin brothers in the Iliad (Book 16), where they carry Sarpedon's body home. The footnote marks the cited lines.
Alpium is a place name near Sparta. Alcander is the young Spartan said to have struck out Lycurgus' eye in a quarrel over his laws.
"From time immemorial" means from a time beyond memory. Ammon's oracle was in the Libyan desert, at the oasis of Siwa.
The expedition against Aphidna was the Dioscuri's (Castor and Pollux) campaign to recover their sister Helen, whom Theseus had carried off.
Theseus was held captive while visiting Thesprotia, and Menestheus gained Athenian support in his absence. Pausanias uses this to doubt that a battle happened.
The pentathlum (pentathlon) was a five-event contest: running, jumping, discus, javelin and wrestling.
The Messenian War refers to Sparta's early wars of conquest against Messenia; the tripods are thus claimed to be very old.
Ægos-potamoi was the 405 BC naval battle where Sparta's Lysander destroyed the Athenian fleet, effectively ending the Peloponnesian War.
"To make therefore a short summary" means Pausanias will list only the scenes, since most myths are well known.
Pausanias notes oddly that the Minotaur is shown alive and fettered, rather than slain, and admits he cannot explain it.
Hera bound by Hephæstus refers to the story that he trapped her in a magic throne as revenge for being cast out of heaven.

context_notes.text: Aphrodite is the goddess of love. Sleep and Death are personified deities, children of Night in Greek tradition.
Lysander was the Spartan admiral who defeated Athens in 404 BC. Aphytis was a town in Pallene, the Chalcidic peninsula.
Alcman was a Spartan lyric poet of the seventh century BC who wrote choral songs for Spartan festivals.
Tripods were bronze cauldrons on three legs, often dedicated to gods as victory offerings.
Bathycles of Magnesia was the sculptor of the Amyclaean throne, a famous archaic monument near Sparta housing Apollo's statue.
Tityus was a giant punished for attacking Leto; Apollo and Artemis, her children, shot him.

literary_notes.text: The story presents Lycurgus as a lawgiver who met violent opposition, yet responded with gratitude to the goddess rather than revenge.
Pausanias steps in with his own judgment, showing his critical, skeptical habit toward local Spartan traditions.
Pausanias speaks as an eyewitness, openly choosing what to omit, which gives the guide authority and a personal tone.
The author's concern about tiring readers shows him shaping the catalogue for an audience, turning description into selective guidance.
Ending with the Trojans' offerings at Hector's grave closes the catalogue of heroic deeds with mourning, a reminder of mortality.
